title: So Close, So Far: Satwiksairaj and Chirag Shetty Fall at the Final Hurdle in Bangkok
excerpt: India's top men's doubles pair claim silver at the Thailand Open after a spirited second-game fightback falls short against Indonesia
body:
At Bangkok's Nimibutr Stadium on Saturday, India's premier men's doubles pair Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty came within touching distance of their first title in two years — only to be denied by Indonesia's Leo Rolly Carnando and Daniel Marthin in a gripping Thailand Open final. The 21-12, 25-23 scoreline tells a story of two halves: a first game where India's top seeds were outplayed, and a second where they mounted a spirited fightback that ultimately fell just short.

## A Final That Promised and Then Denied

The Indian duo, seeded first in the Super 500 tournament, entered the final as favourites after a commanding run through the draw. Their semifinal victory over Malaysia's Goh Sze Fei and Nur Izzuddin — a three-game thriller won 19-21, 22-20, 21-16 — had suggested that the pair were finding the rhythm that once made them the most feared doubles combination in Asia.

The final, however, began disastrously. Carnando and Marthin, the Indonesian pair who have quietly built a reputation as giant-killers on the BWF World Tour, dominated the opening game with clinical precision, racing to a 21-12 victory that left the Indian pair scrambling for answers.

What followed in the second game was a testament to the resilience that has defined SatChi's career. Trailing at multiple points, they clawed their way back into contention, forcing the Indonesians into a nerve-shredding 25-23 finish. The extended deuce rallied the Bangkok crowd, but the final two points went against India.

## India's Sole Medal at the Thailand Open

The silver medal was India's only podium finish at the tournament. Lakshya Sen, the country's top men's singles hope, fell in an earlier round, while PV Sindhu exited in the women's singles quarterfinals to Japan's Akane Yamaguchi — a reminder that India's badminton depth, while growing, remains concentrated in the doubles programme.

For Rankireddy and Shetty, who are ranked fourth in the world, the result carries both encouragement and frustration. This was their first final of the 2026 season, ending a drought that stretches back to the 2025 China Masters. The pair haven't claimed a title since 2024, a dry spell that sits uncomfortably against their résumé: Asian Games gold medallists, Commonwealth Games champions, and holders of the Guinness World Record for the fastest badminton smash at 565 km/h.

## The Diaspora Dimension

Badminton occupies a peculiar space in the Indian sporting consciousness abroad. While cricket dominates NRI sporting conversation, the success of players like Rankireddy, Shetty, and Sindhu has carved out a growing audience — particularly among the South Asian diaspora in Southeast Asia, the Middle East, and the UK, where badminton clubs serve as community gathering points.

The Thailand Open, available on JioCinema and Voot in most international markets, drew substantial viewership from Indian communities abroad. The semifinal victory over the Malaysian pair trended on social media among Indian fans in Singapore and Malaysia, where the diaspora watches with the added intensity of local sporting rivalry.

For NRI parents who shuttle their children between cricket nets and badminton courts on weekends, the success of SatChi offers a powerful counter-narrative: that Indian sporting excellence extends well beyond the 22 yards of a cricket pitch.

## Eyes on Singapore and the World Championships

The road ahead is clear. Rankireddy and Shetty will compete at the Singapore Open and the Indonesia Open in the coming weeks — both tournaments that could define their ranking position ahead of the World Championships later this year.

The Thailand Open silver suggests the pair are trending upward after a mixed start to the season. Their ability to push the Indonesian pair to 25-23 in the second game of a final, after being comprehensively beaten in the first, demonstrates the competitive fire that has kept them in the world's top five for three consecutive years.

For Indian badminton and its growing legion of diaspora supporters, the question is no longer whether SatChi can compete at the highest level. It is whether they can convert near-misses into titles. Bangkok was close. Singapore and Jakarta may prove closer still.
